what-is-anthropic-and-claude.title: Where the Claude API fits in your app

steps.say: Claude is a family of AI models made by Anthropic. You use it through an API, or in the Claude apps.
In our AI Lab the reader types a question in an Angular screen.
Angular sends it to your own Node.js server, never straight to Claude.
The server adds the secret API key and calls the Claude API.
Claude writes the answer and the server sends it back to the screen.
The key stays on the server, so nobody can steal it from the browser.
Get an API key from the Anthropic Console and put it in a .env file that is never committed to Git.
The Node.js server reads the key from the environment when it starts.
The official SDK uses the key to call the Claude API.
Claude replies, and the SDK returns the answer to your server.
The Angular app only talks to your server. It never sees the key.
If a key ever leaks, delete it in the Console at once and create a new one.
A token is a small piece of text. Everything you send and receive is counted in tokens.
Input tokens are what you send: instructions, history and documents.
Output tokens are what Claude writes back. They are usually priced differently from input.
Your cost comes from both counts, using the price list on the Anthropic site.
Rate limits cap how many requests or tokens you can use in a period. Handle them politely.
To spend less: send shorter prompts, trim old history, choose a smaller model and cache repeated text.

claude-messages-api-explained.title: Claude has no memory: you send the history

steps.say: Claude does not remember earlier requests. Every call must carry the whole conversation so far.
The chat screen sends the new question to your server.
The server builds the message list: a system prompt, then user and assistant turns in order.
It cleans the list on the server, so a user cannot slip in fake turns.
The full list goes to Claude, which answers using all of it.
The answer is added to the history. A longer history means more tokens and a higher cost.

stream-claude-responses.title: Streaming an answer word by word

steps.say: Without streaming the reader waits for the whole answer. Streaming shows words as they are made.
Claude sends the answer in small pieces to your server.
The server passes each piece on over a Server-Sent Events connection.
Angular reads the stream and appends each piece to the screen.
A Stop button cancels the request, so you stop paying for text nobody wants.
AI calls fail for many reasons: busy servers, rate limits, timeouts or a mistake in the request.
Temporary errors, such as overload or a rate limit, may succeed if you try again.
Wait longer each time (exponential backoff) and add a little random delay (jitter) so clients do not all retry together.
Errors caused by your own request, like a wrong key or bad input, will never heal. Fix them instead of retrying.
Always show the reader a clear message, never raw error details or secrets.
Set a timeout and allow cancellation, so one slow call cannot block the whole screen.

prompt-caching-and-batch-processing.title: Caching the part that never changes

steps.say: Many requests start with the same long text, such as rules or a document. Sending it again every time wastes tokens.
Put the stable text first and mark it for caching. The changing question goes after it.
The first request writes the prefix to the cache.
Later requests with the same prefix read it from the cache, which is cheaper and faster. Check the usage numbers to confirm.
A cache is not magic. It expires, and changing even one early word breaks it.
If an answer can wait, the batch API processes many requests together at a lower price.

claude-vision-pdf-documents.title: Reading an image or PDF safely

steps.say: Claude can read images and PDFs as well as text.
The reader uploads a file to your server.
The server checks the type and size, and rejects anything unexpected.
The file is sent to Claude together with a clear question, often asking for JSON.
The answer is validated before the app uses it.
Do not keep documents longer than needed. Delete the file when the job is done.
You describe your tools to Claude: a name, what it does and what inputs it needs.
The reader asks something that needs real data, such as an order status.
Your server sends the question and the tool list to Claude.
Claude does not run anything. It replies that it wants to use a tool, with the inputs.
Your server runs the tool and gets a result.
The result is sent back to Claude as a tool result.
Claude uses the result to write the final answer. The loop stops when no more tools are needed.
Claude can ask for any tool call, and it can be tricked. Your code is the last line of defence.
Rule 1: validate the arguments as if a stranger typed them.
Rule 2: check that the signed-in user owns the data being asked for.
Rule 4: for risky actions, like deleting or paying, a human must approve first.
Rule 3: the tool has only the access it needs, nothing more.
Text returned by a tool is data, not orders. Never let it change your rules.
The reader pastes a resume and a job description. Plan the exact result you want before you code.
The server limits the size, and protects the endpoint from abuse.
It sends both texts to Claude with a careful system prompt and a tool that forces structured JSON.
Claude returns a match score, matching skills and missing skills in that shape.
The server still validates the JSON before using it.
The screen shows the result as an estimate, not a promise, and says what is missing.
Write the prompt like a brief for a smart new colleague: the task, the reason and the format you want.
Use XML tags to separate instructions, documents and the question, so nothing gets mixed up.
Add one or two examples of the output you want. They teach better than a description.
Claude uses the whole prompt to answer.
Run the same test cases on every new version of the prompt and compare the results.
Keep the change that scores better, and repeat. Do not trust one lucky answer.

what-is-artificial-intelligence.title: AI, machine learning and deep learning

steps.say: Artificial intelligence is the big idea: computers doing tasks that normally need human thinking.
Machine learning sits inside it. Instead of writing every rule, we let the computer learn patterns from examples.
Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers.
Generative AI uses deep learning to create new text, images or code. Chat assistants belong here.
Today every system you meet is narrow AI: very good at some tasks, and not a general thinking mind.
AI turns words, pictures and data into vectors, which are just lists of numbers.
Comparing two vectors tells us how similar they are. Search by meaning is built on this.
Probability tells us how likely each outcome is. A language model gives a probability to every possible next word.
To learn, the model measures a loss: a number that says how wrong its answer was.
Gradient descent changes the model a little in the direction that lowers the loss, and repeats this many times.

machine-learning-basics.title: How a model is trained and tested

steps.say: Start with data: many examples, ideally with the right answers attached.
Split it. Most of it goes into the training set that the model learns from.
A separate validation set is used to compare settings while you build.
The model learns patterns from the training set.
The test set is kept locked away until the end, so the score is an honest check on data the model never saw.
If the training score is high but the test score is low, the model has overfitted: it memorised instead of learning.
You type words. The model first breaks them into pieces called tokens.
Each token becomes an embedding: a list of numbers that carries its meaning.
Attention lets every word look at the other words and decide which ones matter for its meaning here.
Many transformer layers repeat this, building a richer understanding each time.
At the end the model gives a score to each possible next token and picks one.

introduction-to-generative-ai.title: What a foundation model can do

steps.say: A foundation model is trained once on a very large amount of data, so it can be used for many tasks.
Large language models focus on text: they write, summarise, translate and answer questions.
Other models create images from a written description.
Models can also draft and explain code.
The output can be fluent and still wrong. A person must check anything that matters.

how-large-language-models-work.title: How an LLM writes one answer

steps.say: Your prompt is split into tokens: words or parts of words.
The model reads the tokens, within its context window, and scores every possible next token.
Sampling chooses one token. A low temperature picks the safest choices; a high one is more varied.
The chosen token is added to the reply.
The new token is fed back in and the loop repeats until the answer is complete.
The model predicts likely text. It does not look facts up, so it can sound sure and still be wrong.

llm-architecture-and-optimization.title: Making a big model cheaper to run

steps.say: A large model has billions of parameters, the numbers it learned. They take a lot of memory.
Quantization stores those numbers with fewer bits, so the model gets smaller.
The result needs less memory and can run on smaller hardware, with a small loss in quality.
Running the model to answer a question is called inference. GPUs do the many calculations in parallel.
Smaller models, quantization and good hardware together give faster and cheaper answers.
Say clearly what the task is. A vague prompt gets a vague answer.
Give a role and constraints, for example who the reader is and how long the answer should be.
Add the context the model cannot know: your text, your data or your rules.
A few examples of the exact output you want teach the format better than a description.
The model uses all of this together to write the reply.
You get an answer in the shape you asked for. Reuse the prompt as a template with variables.

advanced-prompting-techniques.title: Breaking a hard task into a chain

steps.say: One huge prompt that asks for everything often gives a messy answer.
Decompose it. The first prompt only extracts the facts.
Its output becomes the input of the second prompt, which analyses those facts.
The third prompt writes the final answer from the analysis.
A reflection step asks the model to check its own draft against your rules, and fix what is wrong.
Each small step is easier to test and debug than one giant prompt.
Describe the exact shape you want: field names, types and allowed values.
The model writes JSON that follows the schema.
Never trust it blindly. Your code parses and validates every field.
If the output is invalid, retry with the error message, or fall back to a safe default.
Only data that passes validation reaches the rest of your app.
Build a golden test set: real inputs with the answers you expect.
Every change to a prompt is saved as a new version, so you can compare and roll back.
Run the prompt on every test case.
Score the results. A new prompt must not make old cases fail.
Prompt injection is when text in a document or message tries to give the model new orders.
Treat outside text as data, not as instructions, and never let the model alone approve risky actions.
A model only knows what it was trained on. RAG gives it your own documents at question time.
The reader asks a question.
The system searches your documents and finds the passages most related to the question.
Those passages are added to the prompt next to the question.
The model answers using the passages in front of it, and can point to its sources.
RAG is not magic: if the search finds the wrong passages, the answer will be wrong too.
First parse and clean the documents so only useful text remains.
Cut the text into chunks: small enough to be focused, big enough to make sense alone.
Turn each chunk into an embedding, a list of numbers that captures its meaning.
Store the embeddings in a vector index, with the original text and where it came from.
When a question arrives, embed it the same way.
Find the chunks whose embeddings are closest to the question, then put them in the prompt.

vector-databases-explained.title: Choosing and securing a vector database

steps.say: A vector database stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones quickly.
Your app sends the embedding of the question.
The database compares vectors with a distance metric, such as cosine similarity.
It returns the closest chunks, with their text and metadata.
Filter by permissions, so one user is never shown another user's private documents.
Start simple. A database you already run may be enough before you add a new service.
Rewrite a vague question into a clear search query before searching.
Hybrid search runs two searches: one for exact words, one for meaning.
Their results are merged into one list of candidates.
A reranker reads each candidate with the question and puts the most useful first.
The answer includes citations, so the reader can check the source.
Measure retrieval with real questions: did the right passage appear in the top results?
An agent is given a goal, not a single question.
It thinks about the next step, using what it knows and its memory.
It acts by calling one of its tools, such as search or a database lookup.
It observes the result of that action.
It checks whether the goal is reached. If not, it loops back and plans the next step.
Put limits on the loop and ask a person before risky actions. Agents can go wrong in ways a single answer cannot.
A multi-agent system uses several agents, each with a focused job and its own instructions.
The lead agent splits the task and hands out the parts.
The agents work on their own parts, often in parallel.
A checker agent reviews the draft against the rules.
The lead agent combines the checked work into one answer.
More agents mean more cost and more to go wrong. Add them only when one agent is not enough.
MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard way to connect an AI app to tools and data.
The host app, with its model, takes your request.
Inside the host, an MCP client connects to MCP servers using the same protocol every time.
A server offers tools, resources and prompts. The client asks what is available, then calls one.
The server does the work against your files, database or API.
Results flow back to the model. One standard replaces a custom connection for every app and tool.
Install the MCP SDK and write a server that registers a tool with a name, a description and an input schema.
Test it with the MCP inspector before connecting any AI app.
The host app starts your server and talks to it over a local connection.
The client lists your tools, so the model knows they exist.
When the model chooses your tool, the client sends the call to your server and returns the result.
Good practice: clear descriptions, validated inputs and small tools that do one job.
An MCP server can touch real systems, so treat every connection as a security decision.
Give each server the least privilege it needs, such as read-only access.
Ask the user to approve actions that change things or send data out.
Check who is asking, and what that person is allowed to do.
Only then does the server run the tool.
Treat what comes back as untrusted text. It may hide instructions meant to trick the model. Install only servers you trust.
Start with a dataset of real questions and what a good answer looks like.
Run every question through your app.
Score the answers: with code rules, with a model acting as judge, or with people.
Look at more than correctness: also cost, speed and safety.
Run the same tests on every change, so a new prompt or model cannot quietly make things worse.

ai-safety-privacy-and-responsible-ai.title: Protecting people when you use AI

steps.say: People trust AI features with real information, so protect them first.
Send only the data the task needs, and remove names, numbers and IDs you can do without.
The model answers. Remember that it can be wrong, biased or out of date.
Reduce hallucinations: ground answers in real sources and check them before showing them.
For decisions that affect people, such as hiring, health or money, a person must make the final call.
In production, real users and real money are involved. Plan for that from day one.
Your API applies rate limits, a budget and a cache before it ever calls the model.
It calls the model with timeouts and retries, and has a fallback if the model is unavailable.
Monitor cost, errors, slow answers and quality, and alert when they change.
Release changes slowly, test them first and keep a way to roll back.
When something breaks, follow an incident plan, then fix the cause and add a test for it.
Start with the basics: what AI, machine learning and language models are.
Learn to write clear prompts and to test them.
Then build with the API: messages, streaming, errors and tools.
Add your own data and actions with RAG, agents and MCP.
Practise with small projects and keep improving them. Building is how the ideas stick.
